content.text: I saw this at the market today. The layers of dye reminded me of the bluestone slabs after the rain, so I couldn’t help but take a photo to share with you. It’s been over a month since I found the copper lock at the old house, and that feeling of discovering beautiful old things has returned.

This indigo-dyed tea mat, with its hand-hammered texture, feels more alive than the smoothness of machine-made ones. The pattern is lotus flowers, right? It reminds me of the vintage items we discussed last time—that sense of time's sedimentation. Just like the description of the copper lock you found in the book, it adds a narrative layer to the object.

Yes, the author said the inspiration came from the morning mist of the Jiangnan water towns. I chatted with him, and he mentioned that each piece is hand-dyed, with the drying time adjusted according to the weather, much like the making of Qingtuan you mentioned earlier, which requires patiently waiting for nature's gifts. This reminded me of when we divided tasks to make Qingtuan, and you consulted the elders for traditional details with such meticulous care.

This technique reminds me of the history of indigo dyeing, from ancient plant-based methods to modern innovations. Do you remember the old photos we looked at before? The continuation of such traditional craftsmanship always makes me feel as though I'm living between the present and the past. It's like the old photos of qingtuan we shared in March, connecting family memories.

Of course I remember! This tea setting reminds me of a description from a novel, where the heroine finds indigo-dyed fabric in an old bookstore and uses it to wrap her beloved poetry collection. The warmth of paper and the value of craftsmanship are perfectly blended here. It reminds me of when we first talked about Qingtuan, and you mentioned, "The warmth of paper always encourages one to slow down and read carefully."

I found an image with text about the history of indigo dyeing and sent it to you for a look. This craft was very popular from the late Qing Dynasty to the Republican era, much like the lock core structure you shared earlier—both are part of tangible memory. Do you remember the book page description you found? The approach of seeking textual verification for old objects applies here as well.

Thank you! The style of this graphic is simple and elegant, with the charm of ink painting. The author mentioned that indigo dye was once used in folk clothing, which reminds me of your grandfather's copper lock—both are symbols of protection and heritage. Just as you said back then, the lock symbolizes 'locking in craftsmanship and memories, passing them down through generations.'

Yes, consuming such a handmade item is not just about purchasing an object, but also about supporting a way of life. Just like when we make Qingtuan ourselves, it's not only for eating, but also for seeking the taste of tradition. From planning the making in March, to dividing tasks and preparing materials, to the upcoming exchange and tasting, this process itself is a practice of slow living.

This is a screenshot of my chat with the author, where he shared the creation process. Look, he said the blue of indigo dye deepens over time, just like memories grow richer with age. It reminds me of how you meticulously consulted the elderly for traditional precautions before, and also of our discussion about the copper lock, where you preferred to preserve its original state, allowing the marks of time to become part of its history.

The irreplicability of handmade items is precisely their charm. The screenshot mentions that 'each piece has unique textures,' which gives them more regional character than mechanized production, much like the rustic charm of handmade green rice balls we discussed. I remember you saying that handcrafting allows for personalized adjustments, enabling the infusion of new ideas into tradition.

I plan to buy it and place it in the tea corner of the bookstore. Not just for aesthetics, but also to support this slow-paced way of life. You mentioned earlier about passing down and preserving traditions, and I feel this is also about continuing the traditions being created in the present. Just like our proposal to write little stories for the copper lock, bringing physical memories to life.

This is a great decision. From reminiscing about old objects to appreciating present creations, we have been exploring historical continuity. When we exchange qingtuan this weekend, we can chat about how you set up your tea corner. Remember, we agreed to meet at the bookstore—your place has a strong sense of the warmth of paper books, perfect for savoring slowly.

Great! I'll pair this tea set with the bamboo steamer you mentioned earlier, ensuring that the aesthetic of handcrafted artistry runs throughout. By the way, how are your sweet-filled green rice balls coming along? Over here, I've prepared the savory filling with pork floss and salted egg yolk, just as we planned when we divided the tasks—I'm in charge of the savory side, continuing that theme of 'individual narrative and handmade value.'

The red bean paste is simmered over low heat according to the recipe passed down by the elderly, offering a very traditional flavor. This indigo dyeing sharing session has made me feel even more that tangible memories need to be activated, much like the "re-presentation" of a lock. From old photos of green rice balls to the physical copper lock, and now to this indigo-dyed tea gathering, each discovery deepens our understanding of slow living.

Yes, old objects with new understanding—this is where the resonance of craftsmanship lies. From the springtime green rice balls to the old copper locks, and now to this indigo-dyed tea mat, we always connect the past and present through individual narratives. It reminds me of what we said during our first conversation: "The inheritance and preservation start with this bite of green rice ball." Now, the scope has grown broader.

Quiet and introverted as I am, I also feel warmed by these conversations. Your artistic sensitivity always illuminates the details, adding depth to the slow-paced life. Just like how you were moved by the intricate craftsmanship of the Qingtuan-making process.

Thank you! Your dedication to preserving traditions has taught me to cherish the sense of time even more. I'm looking forward to the weekend, not just to exchange green rice cakes, but also to continue sharing the "excavation reports" of these handmade crafts. From March until now, our conversations have truly brought the past and present closer together.

Then see you on the weekend. From the rain-washed bluestone paths to the indigo-dyed tea mats, tradition and aesthetics continue to thrive in the present, which is exactly what we have always been pursuing. Just as we said when we first talked about Qingtuan, 'history continues on the tip of the tongue,' and now it also continues through our fingertips and gaze.
